notes: The stranger's survival notes (D-72): a readable book they start with. Basics anyone from the future would know, written for this world. Each entry's 'facts' are keys of material_facts in materials.json; the book prints those facts themselves under 'How it works here', so the book, the judge and the device say the same thing. Advice, not recipes: every attempt is still judged, nothing is keyed to these words, and it covers no way into the city. The reader adds a last chapter, 'Things you've made', from the journey's own journal.
title: Survival Notes
intro: A pocket notebook that came through with you, its pages soft with handling. The basics you'd want in a world without matches, clean taps or a chemist's shop.
This world keeps its own laws. Where these notes quote how something works here, believe it over what you remember.
Whatever you make, the notes keep: the last chapter fills in as you go.

recipes.name: Fire from flint and steel
need: a piece of flint
a piece of steel (a smith's file, a steel blade or a billet of steel; plain iron won't do)
fine dry tinder (dry grass, thistledown, shredded dry bark)
kindling (dry twigs)
fuel (sticks, then split wood)
steps: Loosen the tinder into a nest the size of your fist and set it where the wind can't reach it.
Hold the flint with a sharp edge up and strike down along it, hard and glancing, with the steel, so the sparks fall into the nest.
When a spark catches and smoulders, lift the nest and blow gently until it flames.
Lay the flaming nest down and feed it twigs, then bigger sticks, then wood.
recipes.say: strike the flint against the steel over the nest of dry grass, blow the spark into a flame and feed it twigs and then sticks
recipes.good_for: Warmth, light, boiling water, cooking, hardening wood and clay. The first thing to have.

recipes.name: Borrowing a fire
need: someone else's fire (a hearth, a cooking fire, a forge)
something to carry flame or heat (a torch, a stick, a pot)
steps: Ask first: a fire is someone's work and fuel.
Light a stick or torch at it, or heat what you need right there.
recipes.say: ask if I may light a torch at the fire
recipes.good_for: When you have no steel. Most heating and cooking can simply be done at a fire that's already burning.

recipes.name: Making water safe to drink
need: a pot or kettle that can stand heat
water
a fire
steps: Fill the pot with water from the cleanest source you can find.
Set it over the fire and let it boil hard for several minutes.
Take it off and let it cool before you drink it or wash a wound with it.
recipes.say: fill the pot with water and set it on the fire to boil
recipes.good_for: Killing what sickens people in water. Dirty water stays dirty; boiled water is safe.

recipes.name: Carrying water
need: something that holds water (a bucket, a gourd, a pot, a bowl)
steps: Fill it at a trough, a well or the river.
Carry it upright; pour it into another vessel or where it's needed.
recipes.say: fill the bucket with water from the trough
recipes.good_for: Water goes where its container goes, and nowhere without one.

recipes.name: A clean bandage
need: clean linen or cloth
boiled water, cooled (for washing)
steps: Wash the wound with boiled, cooled water.
Tear the linen into a strip.
Wrap it firm but not tight: fingers should stay warm and pink.
recipes.say: tear the clean linen into a strip and bind the cut with it
recipes.good_for: Stopping bleeding and keeping dirt out of a cut.

recipes.name: A plantain poultice
need: plantain leaves
something to crush them in or with (a bowl, a stone)
a strip of cloth to hold it on
steps: Crush the leaves into a wet green pulp.
Lay it on the burn, sting or cut.
Bind it on with the cloth and change it once a day.
recipes.say: crush the plantain leaves into a poultice and bind it on the burn with a strip of cloth
recipes.good_for: Soothing burns and stings, and helping small wounds stay clean.

recipes.name: A sharp edge from flint
need: flint
a hard stone to strike with
steps: Strike the flint's edge with the stone, glancing, to knock off a thin flake.
Keep the flake with the sharpest edge; blunt the back on the stone so it's safe to hold.
recipes.say: knock a sharp flake off the flint with a hard stone
recipes.good_for: Cutting cord, vine, bark, cloth and saplings.

recipes.name: Moving something too heavy to lift
need: a long stout pole (a lever)
a solid stone or log (a fulcrum)
or rollers, or a rope and helpers
steps: One person lifts and carries about 20 kg on their own; past that, use a tool or other people.
Lever: put the pole under the load, over the fulcrum close to it, and press down on the far end.
Rollers: lever the load onto round logs and roll it, moving the back log to the front.
People: ask for help, and lift together on a count.
recipes.say: lever it up with the long pole over the stone
recipes.good_for: Anything stuck or too heavy: a cart in mud, a beam, a boulder.

recipes.name: Lashing things together
need: cord, vine, rope, leather thongs or rawhide
steps: Wrap the joint tightly many times, crossing over itself.
Finish with a few turns between the two pieces to cinch it, and tie off.
Rawhide put on wet shrinks as it dries and holds hardest of all.
recipes.say: lash the two pieces together tightly with the cord
recipes.good_for: Handles, frames, hafting a blade or a head to a shaft.
